projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with William A. Sloan was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: This interview is being conducted at the Aley United Methodist Church at 4143 Kemp Road, Beavercreek, Ohio and we're interviewing William Sloan. I'm Bob Lindhardt, conducting the interview, and also present is Gary Coffman, who is operating the camera, his wife, Karen, and my wife, Diane. I'm going to be moving over here so that we can focus on you, but don't worry about the camera. We'll get on with the interview here.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: We'll give it a shot.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Is it William Sloan? Do you have a middle initial?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes, A.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: A.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Alfred.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: And your date of birth is?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: [birth date redacted].

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: And you were born where?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: In Arkansas City, Arkansas. Not a very big town, but it is still there.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: And what is your current address?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: [birth date redacted] Beavercreek, Ohio 45432.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: And you were a veteran of World War II?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Correct.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: What was your branch of service?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: The Air Force. Of course, started in the Army Air Corps, 1947 became the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: We'll be getting some of the basic background first. Before we started you mentioned that you had entered through the Aviation Cadet Program, and could you give us a little bit of background?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: It was a yearlong -- it had been a life-long ambition of mine, since a little kid. That is really all I ever thought about doing as a career as I grew up, and was extremely fortunate that it worked out. I was in college at Auburn University for about three years. I was old enough to apply for the program, and in October or November of 1941, we had a reporting-date, sometime in January. And then, of course, Pearl Harbor happened. It was in the spring -- I don't remember exactly, but it seems to me it was probably March or April that everything came to a head and I was enlisted in the Army Air Corps and appointed as a Flying Cadet. I was sworn-in [ inaudible ] started through the process at that point.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Where did you go to your first assignment then?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: First assignment was to Kelly Field in Texas. They had a holding - and stayed at Kelly for probably six weeks and just really basic drills, things of that sort. Then they moved us over to Randolph Field and same sort of thing, just basic marching drills and then getting paid for fledging flight services, training with doctors for flight services. So they got a group of us and marched us over to the hospital and we'd take flight physicals all day long. Then we moved back to Lackey -- [ inaudible ] and we were second class of Flying Cadets to be assigned to Lackey and pre-flights -- just again a lot of marching, academics were flying and grounds crew and basis training. That lasted -- I don't remember for sure, I think probably 12 weeks. Then we moved from there to our first flying assignment. In that case it was a brand-new facility in Texas and that is where we started our flying training. Contract operation, I think there were about six Officers stationed there with airmen for support. All flight instructors. So we had to account for our flying time -- very strict. You had 60 hours' --

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: What kind of an aircraft?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: We were the flying PT-19. [ inaudible ] This assignment ,just as a side note, the first landing I ever made on pavement was one special flight they gave us just before we graduated Flight Service. [ Inaudible ] we went through and graduated into bigger airplanes. Kind of a transition time there, following three different types of airplanes. All assembled -- similar size, similar horsepower, just different factors, different ages.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: This was still training -- general pilot's training? You hadn't been selected for any specialty?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: At this point it was just basis. When we graduated from basic, those who were in multi-engine training [ inaudible ] it was conducted at Kelly, and we were flying twin-engine aircraft, a Beechcraft, which is no longer -- and the only one I know of now was constructed locally -- it's in the museum here. It's a very faithful reproduction. [ Inaudible ]

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Something like the C-45?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Very similar to the C- 45. Very similar section of wing at that time.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: After you finished your advanced training, then where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Of course, the graduation ceremony in San Antonio, and it was a mass graduation on the 7th of December, 1942 [ Inaudible ] and the graduation speaker was the Commander of the Army Air Force. [ INAUDIBLE ] We went from there --

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: You said that was a special situation for you?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes, it was. I thought it was actually going to be held on the 14th of December, which is approximately my birthday. So December 7th was certainly more than the date of the 14th, but the General -- in addition to being the keynote speaker at the graduation, three Representatives from various classes. I was fortune enough to be one of those. [ inaudible ]

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Better having it on. Tell me about it.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: I'm taking the glasses off, because I went to see the ophthalmologist this morning. Okay. You want some words to go with this?

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Tell me about it.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: This is the graduating class from Randolph, class of 42k and the people who completed their basic training at Randolph, and this is a graduation picture. Going to advanced training, which was several in the Air Force -- the type of training that we received.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: You are in that picture?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes, I'm in the picture, just about here. I was very happy. I was married about six weeks at that point and passed major milestones in my training.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: That was a good day?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: That was a good day.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Okay. Why don't we go ahead and get a picture of where you got your wings? Let's see if we can find that one, too.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: This is a picture of graduation classes of 1942 and in the case of the group from Kelly, We were called the 42-K, which was just the designated - [ inaudible ] and when we started and when we were expected to finish. The graduation ceremony itself was held in the auditorium, which is the building just below here. And the massive humanity was all of the cadets from the training fields from the vicinity [ inaudible ] that already had their graduation ceremony.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Interesting headline, "Adolph Hitler won't be happy about this."

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes. [ Inaudible ] [laughter ]

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Let's go ahead with the interview. Okay. After you graduated from your advanced training, were you deployed overseas then?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: No, we went for further training. The group I was -- in fact, the entire class from Kelly Field was stationed -- was transferred to Avon Park, Florida. Of course - [ inaudible ] which is one of the two places in the United States where they were conducting training on the MartinB-26 Marauder. The Air Force Base, which was in Tampa and Avon Park was out in the middle of Florida and also was east of Tampa. From there we got our transition into the Martin. Recruit training, we were put together as a crew after a few hours, and did some crew-training and basic requirement at that point was first pilot flew 100 hours in the Martin before going overseas. Later in the training program, after I came back from overseas, they were still training people in Martin B-26s, but at that time they came to crew training with pilots having at least 200 hours in the airplane before they ever let them start forming the crew and additional training before they shipped them overseas. So probably contrasted to what we had -- we had to scrounge -- I was a co-pilot. So we had to scrounge pretty hard to get a pilot up to 100 hours so we could get shipped out. When we met that goal and they sent the crew to Hunter Field in Savannah, Georgia and that's where we picked up an airplane and ferried across the southern route, across the Atlantic.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: I have heard a lot of stories about the Marauder being a difficult aircraft to fly; any special feelings about the aircraft?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes, I think it was one of the greatest airplanes every built, certainly good framework, and it certainly once a person learned to fly, there wasn't anything significantly different between flying it or any other high-performance multi-engine airplane. It got a bad reputation, and once you get a bad reputation it's often hard to get rid it of. Once-a-days in Tampa Bay, it was a good airplane. It was a good, honest airplane. Let me illustrate that with a short story: A friend of mine was flying in formation with us on a mission in Naples, Italy. He took a hit in the left engine and it was significantly bad it caused the left engine to cease operating, and the left main landing gear, which was housed in the engine itself , extended. He is sitting 10,000' over Naples in a airplane with an unsavory reputation for its performance on a single-engine. He is on a single-engine, and he's got a wheel hanging out, which is tremendous [ inaudible ] He crash-lands that airplane on the beach across the Mediterranean. He lost 10,000' in the process and pretty good pilot, too, he got it across the Mediterranean. That is just an example of how the thing performed in combat. Don't know people that flew it for very long that didn't fall in love with it.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: It's a high-performance aircraft?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Of course it is, yes. It had 4,000 horsepower.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: That ferrying the aircraft to Europe, that was quite an adventure in itself, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes. We picked the airplane up in Hunter at Savannah, as I said, and flew into -- down into Florida to get closer to Puerto Rico-- as we're going from the airport -- we got down closer to Florida, as close as we could in Florida and ferried across to the field in Puerto Rico. We had a little mechanical difficulty there, and wound up staying about four, five days and then we went down to Georgetown. And from there on down to Natal, Brazil. When we picked up the airplane and started ferrying, they took part of our crew and sent them by other transport across to North Africa. So we had a four-person crew. Some of us had a flight engineer and some of us had a navigator, but nobody had both.. So we had a navigator. So when we got to Natal, and arrived at Natal single-ship, just came in and no other way to do it. When we got to Natal, they formed flights of six, for the flight across to Ascension Island, about 8-and-a-half-hour flight, looking for a two-to-four square mile piece of rock out in the middle of the Atlantic that got your attention. So they ensured there was at least one navigator in each flight of six. We had the flight engineer -- some instances[ inaudible ] but we all made it to Ascension. From Ascension we went to the Gold Coast in Africa, and went through around the edges of the desert, Marrakesh. Between Marrakech and Iran. Once we got across the ocean -- [ inaudible ] Iran is where we turned our airplane in.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Do you have a picture of that aircraft?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes, I do. Everybody got to name the airplane, but you only got to name him once. If somebody else had named it, you lived with the name. And whereby [ inaudible ] by acclimation, we decided to call ours "Fly Baby."

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: I'm sorry?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: The airplane.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: What was the name?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: "Fly Baby."

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: "Fly Baby."

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes, and the three people just above it are the three crewmembers, enlisted crewmembers that were part of our combat crew.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: That was the flight engineer -- and?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Flight engineer, a radio operator, and a tail gunner. The flight engineer did the duty -- gunner, and the radio operator, and [ inaudible ] From Iran, we were there for probably a couple of weeks. We had already been assigned to the 319th Bomber Group at that time, and a way to get to Laghouat, which is in Algiers, where the 319th Bomber Group was. They had a big depot operations going on as the airplanes, as they came in, and stripped guns out of them and made them combat-ready. So initially they gave us another airplane, which we took it on up -- on occasion we took it to [ inaudible ] in doing a combat operation [ inaudible ] few days before we moved to another hillside in Algiers. We were there -- I think, I flew my first combat mission from there. We moved twice more after that and moved up to an airfield, Hergla, which was just outside of Tunisia. We operated from there and the war was moving north. So we were pretty far away and they moved us to Sardinia.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: You mean you flew your first combat missions, what were the targets at that time?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: We were bombing targets, both chips and Sicily. Actually my first mission I went as a gunner. I was scheduled to go as a flight crewmember. So I got a shot at gunner [ inaudible ]

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: What was your most dreaded kind of a mission? What were the ones that you --

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: The ones that had a lot of fire-fights.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: What were the targets best -- most heavily guarded?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: As time went by [ inaudible ] warships. Our group was chosen as one of those - one of the groups chosen to bomb the City of Rome. They were extremely careful not to damage the Vatican in any way, damaging artifacts that Rome is known for. So there were strict orders as to how we conducted the mission. [ inaudible ] Our group was one of those chosen -- it was a pretty slick operation. Probably the worst were with the invasion of Italy. We did a lot of support of troops early on the beachhead, those were probably the worst.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: What kind of aircraft did the Germans use at that time?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: They were using mostly F-109s. A lot more 109s than anything else. 109s were usually better pilots [ inaudible ] towards the end of our operation, we did some in Southern France preparing for the invasion of Southern France and there we ran into twin-engine Messerschmitts. They could fire big rockets in formation and we couldn't shoot back at them.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Which was the thing that you dreaded the most? The flak or the aircraft, the fighters?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Well, the flak was more pervasive. So I guess that was more of a concern for -- we had escort most of the time. They used fighters -- not at-bay, but they would keep them active so they could make multiple passes and pass through in formation and come back around and try again.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: When we talked with Max, he was on a B-17 and thought that flak was the thing he dreaded the most.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes, as I say, it was more pervasive. I talked one night with an American anti-aircraft artillery Officer who said, you are bombing at 10,000' and making one-minute bombing runs before you release the bombs? I wish I could get some targets like that. We felt that was not the safest place in the world. As far as I was concerned, it created the problem -- it scared me.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: You had a picture of your aircraft that you were flying over there earlier, too. Do you have that available now?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: As I said earlier, we of course, they took our airplane away from us when we got into Iran, to the depot. This wasn't the one they gave us, but this is the one -- I went through an apprenticeship, like most people did. I was co-pilot for several missions before I got a crew of my own. And this was the airplane that I got approved on. It was a good airplane. It flew beautifully. Just loved the ground a little bit and didn't want to go off quite as early as the rest of them. It turned out to be a benefit when we were doing the six abreast takeoffs. Because you wanted the leader of the flight to stay on the ground, while the other five airplanes were airborne and he could takeoff. So when I got to lead the flights, that was good news, because I didn't have to work that -- I got to stay there. Once it was in the air, it was good or better than good, most of them.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: What was the name of your aircraft?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: "The Sirocco." I don't know that you can see it here, but it's the hot air out of the desert.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: That's an appropriate name.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: [ INAUDIBLE ] Other people flew -- you didn't have an exclusive airplane. I think some of the fighter guys got exclusive airplanes, but we didn't have enough airplanes to go around.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: How many missions did you fly before you moved to Italy?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Before we moved to Sardinia?

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: I don't remember exactly, but it was probably 25, somewhere in that vicinity. We spent more time in Sardinia than any other location.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: You mentioned that six abreast takeoffs, how was that different?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Well, as I mentioned earlier, our Group Commander was -- he was a Major, when I first joined the Group. He got in by attrition. He was a Ranking Officer, former Group Commander who came back from a mission and he became the Group Commander, and he was one of the best leaders I have ever known. He eventually wound up becoming Commander-in-Chief in the States. But anyway, we were flying mostly 24 -36-shift formations and to take 36 airplanes all individually and get them joined up into a formation could take as long as 45 minutes. Just circling the vicinity of the airfield until everybody was in formation and he thought that was a waste of time. So when we moved to Sardinia, flying over dirt/gravel field there, and he had oiled-down six parallel runways a little more that a wing span from our airplanes and had us taking us six ships abreast and landing six ships abreast. By doing that we could first flight would be formed six airplanes by the time you made your first turn in traffic. In the time you would have made one trip around the airport, you would have 36 airplanes joined up ready for combat. That way you were gaining half-hour, maybe, as much as 45 minutes in time and distance that you could fly. Of course, it also had its downside, too. We got all of the long missions because we had more fuel than anyone else.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: What kind of target was normally selected for the Marauders?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: We were mostly transportation, Airfield transportation, railroads -- railway marshaling yards, critical bridges and viaducts, highways, bridges; things associated with transportation primarily.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: How long was a normal mission?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: About four hours was a normal mission. I think the longest was 5-and-a-half. About half of our formations abandoned the Airfields before we got home, [ inaudible ] fuel monitors -- total airplanes -- we went to Sardinia, six abreast and that day didn't start out even flight, but ended up even flight. We had six airplanes in the traffic patterns gotten the formation for landing, and I ran out of gas, talking about the plane performance. Stayed in formation six abreast and things weren't too bad performance -- [ inaudible ]

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: You said when it started it was 25 missions then back -- did anyone rotate back then?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: We were supposed to be able - well, 25 missions were supposed to be rotation time. 25 missions. We weren't getting any replacement crews, so they moved it to 50 and said we had a replacement crew at that point. We still kind of celebrated the 25th and the --

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: So when did you finish your tour?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: I flew 71 missions before I finished [ inaudible ] Naples actually. Called the Santa Maria and I think it flew cargo -- [ inaudible ] [laughter ]Actually a banana boat out of Caribbean that they pressed into service with the troop ships, combination of some of the fanciest, 121-122 days to do it. One thing was unanimous across the board was that nobody is going to channel 9 [ inaudible ] I don't know what there was about it

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Something you didn't see?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: A lot of things we didn't see [ Inaudible ]

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Yes. What kinds of food did they serve?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Spam.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Spam? A lot of spam?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Spam with dried eggs, spam with dried potatoes, spam with ketchup and a piece of bread. Fairly strong distaste for spam [ inaudible ] I shouldn't bad mouth, but after a while --

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Did you ever take any vacations, get away from it any R & R over there?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: I had one-week leave -- we had one airplane that was no longer suitable for safety-flying and they had stripped it out, so it could carry more people. I think there were 12, 13 of us, Representatives from each of the squadrons who flew down to Cairo and stayed in Cairo and Alexandria for a week and came back to the real world.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Any other special memories that you have from that time? Any people that stand out in mind besides your Commander? What was your Commander's name?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Polzak.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Polzak.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes, Randy Polzak.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Does have he any relatives that live around here?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: No, I don't think so. He was Commander of the ESD at the time I was assigned [ inaudible ] we did a lot of missions together as a pilot and co-pilot. That was a long time ago.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Yes. And when you had finished your missions, you mentioned something about you flew some administrative meeting trips and things?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes, there was a time when I passed about 60 missions and said [ INAUDIBLE ] and they said okay. no problem, we have got a lot of administrative trips that need to be take And put you to doing that. About ten days, two weeks later I flew back and said put me back on the schedule. It's safer than what you have me doing on the missions. So they did

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: What year? What date was it that you left Europe?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: I don't remember -- it was late-August -- October '42 - '43. I can't remember the year.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: You showed a picture earlier of your wife that you had when you were over there. You had that setup in your room there?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Getting it up on something that I could see it. There was one question In the form that I did want to address. I did have a good-luck charm. She sent me a little 5" bear in a flight suit with a fur collar and take this with you any time you feel the need to jump, he was my good-luck charm -- erode with me the rest of the missions. I didn't have to throw him out

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Do you have a name for him?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: I'm sorry?

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Did you have a name for him?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: No, just the bear.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Did you receive any awards while you were there?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Airmail four, five plus years DFC, of course campaign ribbons for all the various campaigns and New Service Star. The group got [ inaudible ] in support -- recognizing the group support. Every member of the group

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: The DFC, Distinguished Flying Cross, what was the nature of the citation?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Just cited performance actions of the 50th mission -- I was group leader that day, leading the whole Group formation. Got some things right, I guess.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Are there any other things that you can remember that you would like to share?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: I think just about -- it's taken a long time already.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: You mentioned your journal and you kept a record of just your flights that you kept a record of?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: It started out as a journal -- it evolved from the missions. After 50th [ INAUDIBLE ]

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Could we get the journal -- that would be good

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: The young lady is from Alabama that I met in college, Auburn University. I was walking the streets downtown with a friend of hers, and I didn't know that at the time. Saw this young lady crossing the street from the other side [ INAUDIBLE ] a beautiful lady and I said I've got to meet that girl. The fellow I was walking with -- turned out he introduced me.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: So you are still married to Lu?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: August 1942 we got married. That is a story in itself. Yes, still married

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Yes. That is an understatement of something for sure.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: It's been wonderful.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: I had hoped we would be able to film this down at the museum, as you can tell from watching this, Bill is a very humble person. But he was one of the pilots of the Wright B. Flier built right here in Dayton and I know that you can tell an endless number of stories just about that experience.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Yes, we were associated with that operation. Maybe just a clue is that the time I started flying. I had been flying more than 40 years. And never landed any place except for an airport. Sometimes it might not have been the airport that I picked out to start with, but then the first-year of flying I was in cornfields. So it's a little different operation.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: What other assignments did you have in the States during World War II?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Once I came back to the States I went to Lake Charles, Louisiana. I was instructing in B-26s initially and formed another group-- Another airplane not called the 26 -- an A-26 initially. Twin-engine bomber, again. A group could be as few as one, as many as three or four, depending on the configuration of the airplane. So we were transitioning into that airplane and formed a group that had a specialized mission of pathfinders. [inaudible] I joined that group and was training for that operation.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Of the two aircrafts, the Marauder and A-26, which air craft did you prefer?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Hard choice; I have never flown on an airplane that wasn't a good airplane. Obviously occupies a very special place in my world, but the A-26 was a performer. It was. It outperformed the Martin. Or course, it was a generation later. So it was expected. It was a good airplane. One of these days I'll find another. [laughter ]

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Is there anything -- I'm sorry?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Can we take a break?

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: I would like to make the comment I had two loves in any life. Airplanes and my wife.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: We need -- that would be a really good one to sum it up with. I think that story about the -- about your hat in that crash would be a good one that people would find interesting. So maybe we can hit that one and then we need to talk a bit more about your career after.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: After World War II.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Right, just a bit about that, too. So whenever Gary is ready. Let's go ahead and take a look at the picture.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: This is not it.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Let's take a look at some of the pictures. Hold that one up for us.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: This was the Army Air Corps. This was the Army style hat.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: That was what when I was in the Air Force we called "the wheel hat."

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: When I bought this hat I was in the Army, Army Air Corps and that is the Army-style hat. We all had the hat. It was called " the fur felt," the material, which we all wore like that. [ Inaudible ]

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: But you had another hat?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: It was picked up by our airplane in Havana, in unregulated territory. The pilots had a hat -- Bancroft's name of the hat was "the fighter." It was a twill-type of material and the pocket -- it didn't last very long. If I can find a picture of it - and the first thing we did after we got it, dry it out, find a hot shower where we could take a shower and put it around your ears and that is what it was supposed to do. It was kind of marketable, Army Air Force. As was said earlier it turned out to serve a fairly useful role in combat, because they didn't have any flak helmets. As you mentioned earlier, flak was our biggest concern. We did have GF helmets - and headsets that we had on our ears, we found that we put our headsets on over our ears and then put the outside, the exterior of the steel helmet on over that, it worked just beautiful. The front of the hat kept it from knocking forward in your eyes and the protection -- so a concern degree --

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: So most crewmembers wore that as a standard thing?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: Every Officer, standard equipment. Nobody came back to the States ever fussed about it.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: After the war ended, you went ahead to a career in the Air Force. What are some of the assignments that you had?

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: At the end of the war, they offered service members like myself to make a career and flyers were accepted. The Air Force -- became the Air Force in '47. The Air Force sent me to school twice. We initiated the Civilian Institution Program after the World War II, after the War was over. I took advantage of that and went to Polytechnic Institution and stayed there two years and got a Master's Degree in Mechanical Engineering. Went to Sac for a year voluntarily and was offered the opportunity again for another year or two to go back to graduate school. I took advantage of that opportunity and got a Master's Degree in urban I.T. That earmarked me for Research and Development assignments. I was stationed here on two different occasions. The first time with the brand-new master's degree and stayed here for about three years in the business -- went to Auckland and was testing equipment. Three years in Auckland on the beach -- whitest sand -- [ inaudible ] and spent four years out there, conducting weapons systems evaluation tests for our two interceptors, the F-106 and F-101. Conducted those tests at Patterson. Was there for four years [ inaudible ] left here and went to England for another four-year term. The first two years operational reconnaissance, and the last-half I was Chief of Staff of Operations. At that time [ inaudible ] about that time decided -- [ Inaudible ]- stayed for six-months [ Inaudible ] [ INAUDIBLE ]

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: You had two things that were very important to you in your life. You mentioned earlier -- you showed us a picture of your wife.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: My two loves, not in order of importance but my love of airplanes and met my wife the other love of my life, of course

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: It's a good story. I'm glad you shared it with us. One thing I would like to do if we get an opportunity is to finish this at the Wright Flyer Museum. Maybe we can do that later on.

sp.speaker: William A. Sloan
sp.p: One of the reasons is up until now, the airplane is not all together. They are still working on it. But they finally have it -- [ inaudible ] two weeks from Thursday. - so we'll share it with you.

sp.speaker: Robert Lindhardt
sp.p: Thank you, Bill.
